sections.heading: Stop Signs and Common Causes
body: Some signs mean stop using it first and call second. The rest are the usual suspects.

items.title: A breaker that trips again and again
items.text: An overloaded circuit, a short or a ground fault. A breaker is doing its job when it trips. Resetting it repeatedly hides the reason.

items.title: A dead outlet
items.text: Often a tripped GFCI on another outlet, a loose wire behind the plate or a failed receptacle. A garage, bathroom or outdoor outlet may be fed from a different spot than you'd guess.

items.title: A plate that feels warm
items.text: Heat at an outlet or switch usually means a loose or worn connection. Stop using it, keep things unplugged and have it looked at soon.

items.title: Flickering or dimming lights
items.text: A loose connection on the circuit, or a big load such as a compressor starting on the same line. A single room points one direction, the whole house another.

items.title: Buzzing, crackling or a burnt smell
items.text: These are stop signs. Switch off the circuit if you can do it safely and call. If you see smoke or flames, leave and call 911.

items.title: A repair that didn't hold
items.text: Usually the part was replaced and the cause stayed. Tell us what was done and when it came back.

sections.quote: Quick response. Excellent knowledge and service.

sections.heading: An Older House and What It Might Be Hiding
body: Older homes can have wiring laid out for far fewer appliances than a house has today, and a house that's been added onto may have wiring from several eras.

sections.heading: Write It Down Before You Dial
body: A few minutes of notes make the call faster. Write down which outlets or rooms are affected, whether a breaker tripped, what was running at the time, and whether anyone has worked on it before.

If you can do it safely, leave the affected circuit off and unplug what was on it. Don't keep resetting a breaker that keeps tripping. If a plate is hot or something smells burnt, switch the circuit off and call.

sections.heading: How Outdoor Wiring Is Different
body: Outdoor electrical gets rain, ice and a Kansas summer. Fixtures need to be rated for outdoor use, connections need to be sealed, and outdoor outlets and circuits call for ground-fault protection.
Cable that runs underground or along a fence needs the right type, buried or fastened the right way. These are the details that decide whether lights still work after the third winter.

sections.heading: LED and Controls
body: LED fixtures use less power and run cool, which lets you light more of the yard without loading up a circuit. We also handle LED retro-fits for fixtures you already have.
A timer, a photocell or a switch inside the house means the lights come on when you want them, and not every night until someone remembers.
